# orrery.live

> An interactive 3D solar system in the browser. Real planet positions computed from JPL orbital data, comets, spacecraft, a naked-eye star background with constellations, and a time machine covering 3000 BC to 3000 AD. Free, no account, no adverts.

orrery.live shows where the planets are right now, or on any date you choose. Drag to orbit the view, scroll to zoom, and step time forwards or backwards to watch conjunctions, alignments and retrograde loops play out. It includes the eight planets and their major moons, dwarf planets, notable comets, and the trajectories of spacecraft such as the Voyagers and New Horizons. Famous planetary alignments and historical events are bookmarked so you can jump straight to them.

Planet positions are computed client-side from JPL's long-range Keplerian orbital elements (fitted for 3000 BC to 3000 AD) in the J2000 reference frame, with JPL Horizons data for the dwarf planets, moons and spacecraft, and correct planetary spin axes. The star field is the HYG catalogue, and constellation lines are from d3-celestial.

Technical: static site built on three.js, MIT licensed, installable PWA that works offline once loaded. Textures from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0); star catalogue CC BY-SA 4.0.

## At a glance

- Free, with no sign-up, no ads, no cookies and no analytics or tracking scripts. Settings are kept in your own browser.
- Works on phones, tablets and computers, in any modern browser with WebGL. It can be installed as an app, and works offline once it has been opened.
- Shows the Sun, the eight planets, five dwarf planets (Pluto, Ceres, Haumea, Makemake and Eris), 34 moons, four comets (Halley's, Encke, Hale–Bopp and 67P) and five spacecraft (Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10 and 11, and New Horizons), against 1,637 real stars, the constellation figures and the Milky Way.
- Any date from 3000 BC to 3000 AD, the span of NASA JPL's long-range orbital elements. The date picker goes on to 9999 BC and 9999 AD, with a warning that positions there are approximate.
- Accuracy: from 3000 BC to 3000 AD, each planet's direction from the Sun stays within 0.05° of NASA JPL's DE441 ephemeris for Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, and within half a degree for Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune (checked every 10 days). The Moon is within 0.004° of JPL Horizons from 1900 to 2100. It is an educational model, not a professional ephemeris.
- Scale: planet sizes and the gaps between orbits are enlarged so everything can be seen, but every planet's direction from the Sun is real. The Size and Orbits sliders change the view to true scale.
- The night sky page turns the same sky to your own horizon: which planets you can see tonight from where you are, when they rise and set (to within about a minute), and a mode that follows your phone as you point it at the sky. Its positions are within 0.002° of JPL Horizons from 1990 to 2060.
- Made by Adam Woodland in Brisbane, Australia, as a side project. The code is open source under the MIT licence, on GitHub: https://github.com/adamwoodland-personal/orrery.live

## Links

- [Orrery](https://orrery.live/): the app
- [Night sky tonight](https://orrery.live/night-sky/): sky map of tonight from the visitor's own location: which planets are visible after dark, when they are best placed and which way to look, with sunset/sunrise and twilight times, the Moon's phase, 1,637 stars and the 88 constellations; scrub through the night, change date or city, or point a phone at the sky to identify what is there (compass corrected for magnetic declination); covers 1000 to 3000 AD (most accurate 1800 to 2200); runs entirely in the browser, and the location stays on the device unless the visitor chooses to share a link with their exact position (ordinary share links use the nearest town)
- [Where are the planets right now](https://orrery.live/now/): live table of every planet's distance from the Sun and Earth, light time, evening or morning sky, retrograde motion and next opposition, with a top-down map
- [Where were the planets on the day you were born?](https://orrery.live/planets-on-your-birthday/): for a birthday or any date from 1000 to 3000 AD, which planets were in the evening or morning sky or too close to the Sun, the constellation each was in (and the Sun's and Moon's), brightness, distance, retrograde motion, the Moon's phase, how bunched the five bright planets were compared with every day from 1900 to 2100, a top-down map, and the visitor's age on every planet with the date of their next birthday on each; links to the 3D orrery and the night sky for that date. Astronomy, not astrology: it explains why the Sun's real constellation usually differs from the star sign. Link straight to a date with ?date=YYYY-MM-DD, e.g. https://orrery.live/planets-on-your-birthday/?date=1990-05-17
- [Planetary alignments and planet parades](https://orrery.live/planetary-alignment/): upcoming and past planet parade dates (2022 to 2040) with the planets involved and, for each, which planets are too close to the Sun to see on the date and the latitudes where the others can be seen (checked with the night-sky model every 2° from 54°S to 60°N), what an alignment really is (and what a syzygy is: three or more bodies in a nearly straight line), the 1953 BC five-planet gathering in early Chinese records, and links into the orrery and the night sky page
- [Where is Halley's Comet now](https://orrery.live/halleys-comet/): live distance from the Sun and Earth, speed and a to-scale map of Halley's orbit; its next perihelion (28 July 2061, on Earth's side of the Sun), famous returns since 240 BC, and its two annual meteor showers
- [Where is Voyager 1 now](https://orrery.live/voyager-1/): live distance of Voyager 1 from Earth and the Sun, radio signal time, speed and direction (constellation), and the moment it reaches one light-day from Earth (18 November 2026 at 10:16 UTC, per NASA); a to-scale side view of both Voyagers, Pioneer 10 and 11 and New Horizons; its journey since 1977, whether it is still working and whether it has left the solar system; and the same live figures for Voyager 2
- [What is an orrery?](https://orrery.live/what-is-an-orrery/): the meaning and pronunciation of "orrery", how mechanical orreries work (gear ratios, why no tabletop orrery is to scale, and the few, such as Rittenhouse's, geared for elliptical orbits), kinds of orrery, and their history from the Antikythera mechanism to today
- [The perfect alignment?](https://orrery.live/perfect-alignment/): whether all eight planets ever line up in a perfect syzygy (no exact line is known or expected), either all on one side of the Sun (heliocentric conjunction) or along a line through the Sun with planets on both sides; the tightest one-sided groupings in 6,000 years (1596 BC, 40°), in 20,000 years of JPL data (5753 AD, 39°) and in a two-million-year N-body search (863337 AD, 17°); the tightest lines through the Sun (878 AD 15.7°, 3322 BC 13.4°, 141241 BC 8.8°; next 11 July 2079, 22°); how often each level comes in a model that keeps today’s average orbital speeds (one side within 10° about every 54 million years, 5° about once in 3.4 billion; a line through the Sun is about 128 times as common, 5° about every 27 million years, or 100–250 million as a straight line in 3D; model estimates, not forecasts); why the count falls as the sixth power of the angle; and how far ahead any date can be trusted
- [Sitemap](https://orrery.live/sitemap.xml)
